title: Hinduism at a glance
notes: Cited for: no single founder, scripture or agreed teachings ('a family of religions'); the word Hindu from the Sindhu river; most Hindus revere the Veda and share dharma; many Hindus call themselves monotheists.

title: Hindu concepts
notes: Cited for: atman as eternal self; karma as 'action'; samsara; moksha; the goals of life; Brahman; a Supreme God in many forms; ishta devata; God creating and destroying the universe over and over.

title: Hindu scripture
notes: Cited for: Yajurveda and Samaveda used at Vedic sacrifices; the Bhagavad Gita, 'Song of the Lord', as smriti and one of the most popular Hindu texts.

title: History of Hinduism: classical period
notes: Cited for: Vaishnavism, Shaivism and Shaktism developing in the Gupta period (320 to 500 CE).

title: Vishnu
notes: Cited for: the Trimurti roles of Brahma (creator), Vishnu (preserver) and Shiva (destroyer).

title: Hindu worship
notes: Cited for: most Hindu homes have a shrine; offerings of water, fruit, flowers and incense; worship mainly individual; pilgrimage to see and be seen by the deity.

title: Puja: Expressions of Hindu Devotion (background for teachers)
publisher: Smithsonian Institution, Freer and Sackler Galleries
notes: Cited for: puja's three parts (seeing the deity, offerings, receiving blessed food); temple puja at sunrise, noon, sunset and midnight; images bathed and clothed.

title: Hinduism
notes: Cited for: 'Hinduism' coined by British writers in the early 19th century; sanatana dharma, 'eternal law'; three paths to liberation (karma, jnana, bhakti).

title: Artha
notes: Cited for: artha as one of the four traditional aims of life, with moksha (spiritual release) the final aim.

title: Vaishnavism
notes: Cited for: Vaishnavism as a major form of modern Hinduism devoted to Vishnu and his avatars, such as Rama and Krishna.

title: Puja
notes: Cited for: puja as Hindu ceremonial worship, from brief daily rites in the home to elaborate temple rituals.

title: Darshan
notes: Cited for: darshan as beholding a deity (especially in image form), a revered person or a sacred object, a two-way exchange that blesses the viewer.

title: Diwali
notes: Cited for: dipavali, 'row of lights'; five days at the new moon of Karttika; diyas and Lakshmi; Rama's return and Krishna's victory; Jain and Sikh meanings.

title: Holi
notes: Cited for: Holi at the full moon of Phalguna (February or March); colored powders and water; bonfires for Holika; social rankings set aside.

title: Hindu calendar
notes: Cited for: a lunisolar calendar of 12 lunar months (about 354 days) adjusted by extra months, so festival dates shift against the Gregorian calendar.

title: Upanisads
notes: Cited for: four Vedic collections with four layers; oldest Upanishads dated 700 to 500 BCE; Vedanta as 'end of the Vedas'; Uddalaka's salt-in-water lesson and 'you are that'; Yajnavalkya and Shankara on atman and Brahman; the Brahma Sutra on moksha.

title: Jainism
notes: Cited for: Jina, 'conqueror'; Mahavira as 24th and last Tirthankara; ahimsa to all living things; mahavratas for ascetics and anuvratas for laypeople.

title: Jaina Philosophy
notes: Cited for: Mahavira, 'the Great Hero', traditional dates 599 to 527/510 BCE, the 24th and last Jina of the current cosmic period.

title: Jainism at a glance
notes: Cited for: the five great vows; the Digambara ('sky clad') and Svetambara ('white clad') sects.

title: Mahavira
notes: Cited for: Vardhamana, a prince, renouncing at 30 and spending twelve and a half years in fasting and meditation; traditional date 599 BCE, some scholars later.

title: Jain beliefs about the soul
notes: Cited for: jiva in every living thing; one-sensed earth, water, fire, air and plant beings; ants with three senses.

title: Karma in Jainism
notes: Cited for: Jain belief that karma is a physical substance that sticks to the soul through its actions.

title: Ahimsa (non-violence)
notes: Cited for: ahimsa as the most central Jain teaching; saving one's soul by protecting every other soul; harm attracting karma; monks sweeping the ground and wearing mouth cloths.

title: The lay Jain life code
notes: Cited for: lay Jains keeping the five vows as lesser vows: vegetarian diet, filtering water, not eating at night, possessing only what they need.

title: Aparigraha (non-possession)
notes: Cited for: Digambara monks carrying only a whisk broom to sweep insects from their path and a water pot.

title: Jainism
notes: Cited for: the parable of the elephant and the blind men (ear a fan, leg a post, side a wall); a tirthankara as a 'ford builder' who shows others how to cross the currents of life.

title: Eschatology
notes: Cited for: eschatology as Jewish, Christian and Muslim beliefs about the end of history, the resurrection of the dead and the Last Judgment; biblical eschatology directed toward a historical future, other religions' cycles of cosmic destruction and rebirth.

title: How the Major Religions View Reincarnation
notes: Cited for: reincarnation is not an approved doctrine of orthodox Christianity, Islam or Judaism, which hold to one lifetime, one Day of Judgment and resurrection.

title: Islamic beliefs
notes: Cited for: Muslim belief in the Day of Judgement, when every human life will be assessed.

title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Article 7: 'From thence he will come again to judge the living and the dead'
notes: Cited for: the Church's teaching that Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead.

title: Jewish Resurrection of the Dead
notes: Cited for: Maimonides listing resurrection of the dead among his 13 principles of Jewish faith; the doctrine debated throughout Jewish history.
